newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan growth expected to slow next year.
newsitem.headline: Japan growth expected to slow next year.

text.p: Japan's already anaemic economic growth is likely to slow slightly next year, but the country should still enjoy a moderate pace of expansion into the next century, private economists said on Friday.

They forecast, on average, that Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key gauge of the economy's health -- will grow by 1.6 percent in the fiscal year beginning in April after an estimated growth of around 2.5 percent in the current business year.
Some economists were more bullish with forecasts of GDP growth of more than two percent next year.

"The economy looks like it will start overcoming the after-effects of the collapse of the 'bubble' economy next year and will start making a full-fledged recovery in 1998/99," said Tatsushi Shikano, economist at Yamaichi Research Institute.
The institute expects GDP to grow by 1.7 percent in 1997/98, and by an average of three percent in the following three years.
Japan's economy was hard hit by the collapse of the 1980s "bubble" economy of inflated stock and land prices, plunging it into negligible growth from the beginning of 1992 until about mid-1995.
The economists' predictions were made before the government announces next month its official growth estimate for the next fiscal year, which is expected to be rosier than the economists' view.
Government officials have said the official growth forecast would be slightly less than two percent.

The predictions compare with forecasts of GDP growth of 2.7 percent for the United States and 2.4 percent for Germany in 1997. The forecasts were made by the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development in its June report.

The economists said a planned increase in Japan's consumption tax to five percent from three percent from April 1 would restrict growth in the first half of 1997/98, but the economy would would pick up in the second half.
"The consumption tax increase will have a temporary one-off impact," said Andrew Shipley, economist at Schroder Securities (Japan) Ltd. He expects GDP growth of 2.3 percent in 1997/98.
He added he expects private consumption to increase,

"There was a clear sign that the economy had bottomed out in September when for the first time in four years the number of jobs increased among manufacturers," Shipley said. "People spend more when they feel they are more secure on the job."
The economists also dismissed worries that a prospective fiscal tightening by the government to balance the state budget could push the economy back into a recession.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has vowed that he would make 1997/98 the first year of fiscal reforms, pointing to a cut in government expenditures, including public works spending. Public works projects have been traditionally seen as an effective measure to stimulate the economy.
"I think the fiscal tightening has already happened this year. Public works have been exhausted...yet recent economic data has been very strong," said Russell Jones, economist at Lehman Brothers.
"The potential deflationary impact of the fiscal U-turn may well have been exaggerated," Jones said.

One cautionary note, the economists said, was that a continuation of the economic recovery would likely result in the Bank of Japan ending its super-accommodative monetary policy by edging the official discount rate upward in 1997.
The central bank has kept the key lending rate at a historic low of 0.5 percent since September last year.
